Print 1 to N with three threads in turn (T1: 1, T2: 2, T3: 3, T1: 4 ...)

Same idea as odd/even, generalised: each thread waits until (n - 1) % threads equals its id. signalAll is needed because signal might wake the wrong thread, which would go back to waiting and the program would hang. An alternative is one Semaphore per thread, where each thread releases the next thread's semaphore after printing.
Write your own bounded blocking queue with wait/notify (producer–consumer without BlockingQueue)

Rules interviewers look for: wait/notify must be called while holding the object's monitor (otherwise IllegalMonitorStateException); always wait in a while loop, not an if; use notifyAll because producers and consumers wait on the same monitor. A ReentrantLock version with two conditions (notFull, notEmpty) is more efficient because it wakes only the right side; that is how ArrayBlockingQueue works internally.
CountDownLatch and CyclicBarrier: wait for N tasks to finish

| CountDownLatch | CyclicBarrier
Who waits | One or more threads wait for others | The parties wait for each other
Reusable | No (count only goes down) | Yes, resets after each trip
Typical use | Startup, "wait for N results" | Multi-phase parallel algorithms
For a single "wait for all tasks" today, invokeAll or CompletableFuture.allOf is usually simpler. ExecutorService is AutoCloseable since Java 19, so try-with-resources waits for the tasks and shuts it down.
Semaphore: allow at most 3 concurrent calls to a slow API

A semaphore holds a number of permits; acquire blocks until one is free. It limits concurrency (how many at the same time), not rate (how many per second); for a rate limit use a token bucket or a library such as Resilience4j. A semaphore with one permit is like a lock, except any thread can release it. Semaphores are a good way to protect a downstream service when using virtual threads, where the thread count itself no longer limits load.
Thread-safe word count with ConcurrentHashMap (and the check-then-act bug)

Each single method call on a ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe, but a sequence of calls is not. merge, compute and computeIfAbsent lock only that key's bin, so other keys are not blocked. Keep the lambdas short and never modify the same map from inside them. ConcurrentHashMap does not allow null keys or values, because a null from get would be ambiguous.
Read-mostly cache with ReentrantReadWriteLock

Read locks are shared and the write lock is exclusive, so throughput improves when reads far outnumber writes. You can downgrade (take the read lock while holding the write lock, then release the write lock), but you cannot upgrade a read lock to a write lock; trying to do so deadlocks. In real code a ConcurrentHashMap or Caffeine cache is usually the better answer; mention StampedLock for optimistic reads.
Java 21 virtual threads: run 10,000 blocking calls

Virtual threads are cheap JVM-managed threads mounted on a small pool of carrier threads; when one blocks on I/O, it unmounts and the carrier runs another. Use them for many blocking, I/O-bound tasks (one thread per request); they do not make CPU-bound work faster. Don't pool them, and limit access to scarce resources with a Semaphore. Before Java 24, blocking inside synchronized could pin the carrier thread, so ReentrantLock was preferred around long blocking calls. In Spring Boot 3.2+, spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true switches request handling to virtual threads.
CompletableFuture error handling in depth: handle vs exceptionally, completeOnTimeout, anyOf

exceptionally runs only on failure, handle always runs and can transform both outcomes, and whenComplete observes without changing the result. The exception arrives wrapped in a CompletionException, so check ex.getCause(). Always pass your own executor for blocking I/O; the default common ForkJoinPool is sized for CPU work. join() throws unchecked exceptions, while get() throws checked ones.
synchronized vs ReentrantLock: when do you need the Lock?

| synchronized | ReentrantLock
Unlock | Automatic, even on exception | Manual: always in finally
Try without waiting / timeout | No | tryLock(), tryLock(1, SECONDS)
Interruptible wait | No | lockInterruptibly()
Fairness option | No | new ReentrantLock(true)
Wait conditions | One (wait/notify) | Many Conditions (e.g. notFull, notEmpty)
Reentrant | Yes | Yes
Rule of thumb: start with synchronized; switch to ReentrantLock when you need tryLock (deadlock avoidance), timeouts, interruptible waits or more than one condition.
sleep() vs wait() vs join()

| Thread.sleep(ms) | obj.wait() | t.join()
Defined on | Thread (static) | Object | Thread (instance)
Must hold the monitor | No | Yes, else IllegalMonitorStateException | No
Releases locks it holds | No | Yes, that object's monitor | No
Wakes up when | Time passes or interrupted | notify/notifyAll, interrupt, timeout or spurious wake-up | Thread t finishes, or timeout
Typical use | Delays, retries, demos | Hand-written producer–consumer | Wait for a worker thread to finish
Interview tip: always call wait() inside a while loop that re-checks the condition, because of spurious wake-ups and because another thread may have taken the item first.
Runnable vs Callable vs CompletableFuture

| Runnable | Callable<V> | CompletableFuture<V>
Returns a value | No | Yes | Yes
Checked exceptions | Cannot throw them | Can throw | Supplier cannot throw them; failures come out of join() wrapped in CompletionException
Get the result | n/a | future.get() blocks | Callbacks (thenApply, thenCombine) or join()
Chaining / combining | No | No | Yes
Default executor | Yours | Yours | ForkJoinPool.commonPool() unless you pass one
Rule of thumb: Runnable for fire-and-forget, Callable when one task returns one result, CompletableFuture when results must be chained or combined. For blocking I/O, pass your own executor instead of using the common pool.
Hashtable vs Collections.synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap

| Hashtable | synchronizedMap(new HashMap) | ConcurrentHashMap
Locking | One lock for the whole map | One lock for the whole map | Per-bin locks + CAS; reads mostly lock-free
Iterating while others write | ConcurrentModificationException | CME unless you lock the map yourself | Weakly consistent, never throws CME
Null keys / values | No | Yes (HashMap rules) | No
Atomic compound ops | No | No | merge, compute, putIfAbsent
Status | Legacy | OK for low contention | Default choice
Rule of thumb: use ConcurrentHashMap and its atomic methods. Every call on a synchronized map is safe on its own, but "check then put" across two calls is still a race.
shutdown() vs shutdownNow() vs awaitTermination() vs close()

| shutdown() | shutdownNow() | awaitTermination(t) | close() (Java 19+)
New tasks | Rejected | Rejected | n/a | Rejected
Queued tasks | Still run | Removed and returned as a list | n/a | Still run
Running tasks | Finish normally | Interrupted (they must react to it) | n/a | Finish normally
Blocks the caller | No | No | Yes, up to the timeout | Yes, until all are done
Rule of thumb: the usual pattern is shutdown(), then awaitTermination, then shutdownNow() if it timed out. On Java 21, try-with-resources on the executor calls close() for you.
